newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle crew prepares for early return.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle crew prepares for early return.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Columbia shut down their space laboratory on Tuesday, with only a fraction of their $84 million research programme accomplished, and got ready for an early homecoming.
Columbia was due to touchdown at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 2:33 p.m. EDT (1833 GMT). The mission was curtailed by a malfunctioning power generator.
"We're just sorry we're having to close up shop early," mission control's Marc Garneau radioed the crew.

Scientists have requested another shuttle flight for their space laboratory, which was to have studied the behaviour of fire in space, the growth of plants, the structure of proteins and the manufacture of ultra-pure materials.

Weather conditions looked favourable at Kennedy Space Centre and at the backup landing strip in California, although winds were forecast to be gusty at both sites, mission control commentator James Hartsfield said.
The weather was expected to deteriorate at both runways on Wednesday. Winds would be too high and there would be a chance of rain in Florida.
Mission commander Jim Halsell and Susan Still were to fire the shuttle's braking rockets at about 1:30 p.m. EDT (1730 GMT) to begin an hour-long descent through the atmosphere.
The loss of one of the shuttle's three electricity generating fuel cells should not affect the performance of the $2 billion gliding spaceplane.
"Most of our equipment will be running that we require for landing," Still said. Some landing systems will be activated later than usual to conserve power, she explained.
Flight controllers ordered an early end to Columbia's planned 16-day mission because the fuel cell was degrading and in a worst case could have sparked a fire and an explosion.
It was only the third time in 83 missions that a shuttle had been called home early because of a mechanical breakdown.
The fuel cell behaved unusually during Columbia's countdown, but appeared be have returned to normal before Friday's blastoff.
Engineers had seen similar readings before previous missions which later encountered no problems after launch, NASA officials said.
